museums.name: The Louvre
museums.blurb: Five of its key rooms, from the glass pyramid to the Mona Lisa’s.

museums.name: The National Gallery
museums.blurb: On Trafalgar Square: Van Eyck, Constable, Turner and Van Gogh.

museums.name: The British Museum
museums.blurb: The Great Court, the Egyptian sculpture gallery and the Parthenon’s marbles.

museums.name: The Uffizi
museums.blurb: The Medici’s gallery, with Botticelli’s room and the Tribuna.

museums.name: Piazza della Signoria
museums.blurb: Out in the open, before the Palazzo Vecchio: the copy of Michelangelo’s David at its door.

museums.name: The Sistine Chapel
museums.blurb: Michelangelo’s ceiling and his Last Judgment, in the Vatican.

museums.name: The Rijksmuseum
museums.blurb: The Gallery of Honour and the Night Watch at its end.

museums.name: The Prado
museums.blurb: The Spanish kings’ collection: Velázquez, Goya and Bosch.

museums.name: The Kunsthistorisches Museum
museums.blurb: The Habsburgs’ collection, with the most Bruegels anywhere.

museums.name: The Neues Museum
museums.blurb: Egypt on the Museum Island, Nefertiti in her own domed room.

museums.name: The Pergamon Museum
museums.blurb: A Greek altar and the gate of Babylon, rebuilt indoors.

museums.name: St Mark’s Basilica
museums.blurb: Five domes of gold mosaic and the golden altarpiece.

museums.name: St Bavo’s Cathedral
museums.blurb: Ghent’s cathedral, home of the Van Eyck brothers’ altarpiece.

pieces.title: Mona Lisa
pieces.blurb: Leonardo’s portrait of a Florentine silk merchant’s wife, the most visited painting in the world.
text: Leonardo began painting Lisa Gherardini, the wife of the silk merchant Francesco del Giocondo, in Florence around 1503. He never handed it over: he kept working on it for years and took it with him to France, where King Francis I acquired it. That is why it is in Paris, and why the Italians still call it La Gioconda.

It is only 77 by 53 cm. Leonardo blurred every outline into soft shadow (sfumato), so the corners of her mouth never quite settle into a smile, and the landscape behind her does not line up on either side.

On 21 August 1911 a handyman, Vincenzo Peruggia, walked out of the Louvre with it under his smock. It turned up in Florence two years later, and the theft made it the most famous painting in the world. Since 2005 it has hung alone behind bulletproof glass in the Salle des États, opposite the Wedding at Cana.

pieces.title: The Wedding at Cana
pieces.blurb: Veronese’s Venetian feast, the biggest painting in the Louvre, across the room from the Mona Lisa.
text: Veronese painted it for the refectory of the Benedictine monastery of San Giorgio Maggiore in Venice, where the monks ate under it. Christ’s first miracle, turning water into wine, becomes a sixteenth-century Venetian banquet with more than 130 guests, servants, musicians, dogs and a cat.

Napoleon’s troops carried it off in 1797, cutting it apart to roll it up for the journey. When the looted art went back after 1815, the Louvre kept it and sent Venice a painting by Le Brun instead. Nearly ten metres wide, it covers a whole wall of the Salle des États.

pieces.title: The Raft of the Medusa
pieces.blurb: Survivors of a shipwreck wave at a ship on the horizon: a scandal of 1816, painted life-size.
text: In July 1816 the French frigate Méduse ran aground off the coast of West Africa. Its officers took the lifeboats and left some 150 people on a makeshift raft; after thirteen days only fifteen were still alive when the brig Argus found them.

Géricault, 27 years old, interviewed survivors, had a model of the raft built and studied the dying in hospitals and the dead in the morgue. He painted the moment the survivors spot the Argus, a speck on the horizon, and a man waves a cloth at it. Shown at the Salon of 1819, it read as an attack on the government that had given the ship to an incompetent captain.

pieces.title: Liberty Leading the People
pieces.blurb: Liberty climbs the barricade with the tricolour: Delacroix’s picture of the revolution of July 1830.
text: In three days of July 1830 Parisians rose against King Charles X and drove him from the throne. Delacroix, who had not fought, painted it that autumn: Liberty in a Phrygian cap strides over the dead with the flag in one hand and a musket in the other, a boy with two pistols and a man in a top hat beside her, and the towers of Notre-Dame far off in the smoke.

The state bought it in 1831 and then hid it away for years as too inflammatory. It has hung in the Louvre since 1874, and its figure of Liberty became Marianne, the face of the French Republic. A restoration in 2024 took off the yellowed varnish and brought back the blue, white and red of the flag.

pieces.title: Venus de Milo
pieces.room: Gallery of the Venus de Milo
pieces.blurb: The armless goddess found by a farmer on the Greek island of Milos in 1820.
text: A farmer digging among ruins on the island of Milos found her in April 1820, in two pieces and already without arms. A French naval officer saw her, the French ambassador in Constantinople bought her, and she was given to King Louis XVIII, who gave her to the Louvre in 1821.

She is probably Aphrodite, the goddess of love, carved around 150–125 BC. A piece of her base, now lost, bore the name of the sculptor Alexandros of Antioch. Nobody knows what her arms were doing: holding an apple, a mirror or a shield are the usual guesses.

pieces.title: Winged Victory of Samothrace
pieces.medium: Parian marble on a prow of grey marble
pieces.blurb: Nike, goddess of victory, landing on a warship’s prow at the top of the Louvre’s great staircase.
text: Nike, the goddess of victory, alights on the prow of a warship, the wind pressing her wet robe against her body. She stood in the sanctuary of the Great Gods on the island of Samothrace, probably as a thank-offering for a sea battle won around 190 BC.

The French consul Charles Champoiseau dug her up in 1863, in pieces. Since 1884 she has stood on her prow at the top of the Daru staircase, where you see her from the foot of it. Her head and arms were never found; her right hand turned up on Samothrace in 1950.

pieces.title: The Virgin of the Rocks
pieces.medium: Oil on panel, transferred to canvas
pieces.blurb: The Virgin, the infant Christ, the little John the Baptist and an angel in a grotto of rocks and flowers.
text: Leonardo was asked in 1483 by a confraternity in Milan to paint the middle of their altarpiece. In a shadowy grotto the Virgin puts her arm round the infant John the Baptist, who kneels to the infant Christ; an angel looks out at us and points.

The plants growing from the rocks are painted so exactly that botanists can name them. A quarrel over the price followed, and Leonardo painted a second version, now in the National Gallery in London; this first one went to the kings of France.

pieces.title: The Oath of the Horatii
pieces.blurb: Three Roman brothers swear to their father to fight for Rome or die, their sisters weeping beside them.
text: The story is from Livy: to settle a war between Rome and Alba, three brothers from each city were to fight it out. The Horatii hold out their arms to the swords their father raises, while the women give way to grief: one of the sisters is engaged to one of the brothers they will fight.

David painted it in Rome for King Louis XVI and showed it at the Salon of 1785. Its hard light, its bare columns and its few stern figures made it the model of the new classical style, and soon a call to duty for the Revolution.

pieces.title: La Grande Odalisque
pieces.blurb: A nude in a harem looking back over her shoulder, her back impossibly long.
text: Ingres painted her in Rome for Caroline Murat, Napoleon's sister and Queen of Naples, who never got it: the Murats fell with Napoleon the next year.

At the Salon of 1819 the critics laughed at the length of her back, two or three vertebrae too many, they said. Ingres stretched it on purpose, for the line, and the picture became one of the Louvre's best loved.

pieces.title: The Coronation of Napoleon
pieces.room: Salle des États (in the Louvre, the Salle Daru next door)
pieces.blurb: Napoleon crowns Josephine in Notre-Dame, the Pope seated behind him, on 2 December 1804.
text: Napoleon had already set the crown on his own head; David chose the next moment, when the new Emperor crowns the kneeling Josephine, with Pope Pius VII raising his hand behind him. Some 150 people are in it, most of them real portraits.

David was Napoleon's First Painter, and took three years over it. Napoleon's mother is in the gallery in the middle although she stayed away from the ceremony. Almost ten metres wide, it is the second biggest painting in the Louvre, after the Wedding at Cana.

pieces.title: Sunflowers
pieces.blurb: Fifteen sunflowers in a yellow pot, painted in Arles to welcome Gauguin.
text: In August 1888 Van Gogh was waiting in Arles for his friend Paul Gauguin to come and stay in the Yellow House. To decorate Gauguin’s room he painted four pictures of sunflowers in a few days, working fast before the flowers wilted. This one, yellow on yellow, is one of the two he thought good enough to sign, on the vase.
He painted repeats of his sunflowers the next winter, now in Amsterdam, Philadelphia and Tokyo. The National Gallery bought this one in 1924.

pieces.title: The Hay Wain
pieces.blurb: A hay cart crossing the river Stour in Suffolk, under big summer clouds.
text: Constable painted the countryside he grew up in: the river Stour at Flatford Mill, where his father had a mill, with Willy Lott’s cottage on the left and an empty hay cart splashing through the shallows to the fields beyond.

Shown at the Royal Academy in 1821 as Landscape: Noon, it did not sell. In Paris three years later it won a gold medal from King Charles X, and young French painters such as Delacroix studied its fresh greens and broken touches of white.

pieces.title: The Arnolfini Portrait
pieces.blurb: An Italian merchant and his wife in their room in Bruges, and Van Eyck himself in the mirror.
text: Giovanni Arnolfini, a merchant from Lucca, stands with his wife in their house in Bruges: an orange on the windowsill, a little dog at their feet, a brass chandelier with one candle burning in broad daylight.

In the round mirror on the back wall two more people stand in the doorway, one of them probably the painter. Over the mirror he wrote “Johannes de eyck fuit hic 1434”: Jan van Eyck was here. The National Gallery bought it in 1842.

pieces.title: The Fighting Temeraire
pieces.blurb: An old warship of Trafalgar towed up the Thames to be broken up, under a blazing sunset.
text: HMS Temeraire fought at Trafalgar in 1805, second in line behind Nelson’s Victory. In 1838 a steam tug towed her up the Thames to Rotherhithe to be broken up for timber. Turner painted her pale as a ghost behind the black tug, with the sun going down on the other side of the picture.
He called it his darling and never sold it; it came to the nation with his bequest. In 2005 listeners of BBC Radio 4 voted it Britain’s greatest painting, and since 2020 it has been on the £20 note.

pieces.title: The Ambassadors
pieces.blurb: Two young Frenchmen at the court of Henry VIII, between them a table of globes and instruments, and a skull across the floor.
text: Jean de Dinteville, the French ambassador in London, and his friend Georges de Selve, a bishop, stand either side of a shelf of things for measuring the heavens and the earth: globes, sundials, a quadrant, a lute with a broken string.

The grey smear across the floor is a skull, painted in steep perspective: it only takes its shape when you look from close to the frame on the right. Death waits behind all that learning. The National Gallery bought it in 1890.

pieces.title: The Rokeby Venus
pieces.blurb: Venus lying with her back to us, looking at herself in a mirror Cupid holds up.
text: The only female nude by Velázquez that survives, rare in the Spain of the Inquisition. Her face in the mirror is a blur, so she stays nobody in particular.

It takes its name from Rokeby Park in Yorkshire, where it hung in the 19th century. Bought for the nation in 1906, it was slashed with a meat cleaver in 1914 by the suffragette Mary Richardson; the cuts were mended so well they hardly show.

pieces.title: Whistlejacket
pieces.blurb: The Marquess of Rockingham's racehorse, rearing up life size against an empty background.
text: Stubbs had spent eighteen months dissecting horses to learn how they are made, and here painted an Arabian stallion at full size, rearing, with nothing round it at all.

Whether a rider and a landscape were meant to follow is still argued about. The National Gallery bought it in 1997, and it hangs at the end of a long view, so the horse seems to rise over the visitors.

pieces.title: Bathers at Asnières
pieces.blurb: Young workmen resting on the bank of the Seine on a hot day, the factory chimneys of Clichy behind them.
text: Seurat was 24 when he painted it, his first big picture, after dozens of small studies made on the spot. The Salon turned it down, and it was shown at the first Salon des Indépendants in 1884.
A few years later he went back to it and added small dots of pure colour here and there, in the boy's hat for one: the way of painting, pointillism, he went on to invent.

pieces.title: The Water-Lily Pond
pieces.blurb: The Japanese bridge over the lily pond in Monet's garden at Giverny.
text: Monet dug the pond himself in 1893, turning a little river through his garden at Giverny, and put a wooden footbridge in the Japanese style over it.
In 1899 he painted the bridge a dozen times, from almost the same spot. For the rest of his life the lilies on that water were nearly all he painted.

pieces.title: The Rosetta Stone
pieces.blurb: The same decree in three scripts: the stone that let us read Egyptian hieroglyphs again.
text: Priests meeting at Memphis in 196 BC issued a decree in honour of the young king Ptolemy V, and it was carved on stone three times: in hieroglyphs, in Demotic (the everyday Egyptian script) and in ancient Greek.

French soldiers found the broken slab in 1799 at Rashid, which Europeans called Rosetta, built into an old fort. The British took it under the treaty of 1801, and it has been in the British Museum since 1802. Because the Greek could be read, Thomas Young and then Jean-François Champollion worked out the hieroglyphs from it, Champollion announcing it in 1822.

pieces.title: Ramesses II, the Younger Memnon
pieces.blurb: The colossal head and shoulders of Ramesses II, carried from Thebes to London in 1816–1818.
text: The upper part of a seated statue of Ramesses II from his mortuary temple at Thebes, the Ramesseum, cut from one block of granite with a darker and a lighter part, so his face is pink and his body grey.

In 1816 the strongman and explorer Giovanni Belzoni had it dragged on rollers to the Nile and shipped to London; it reached the British Museum in 1818. The news of it is said to have inspired Shelley’s sonnet Ozymandias, about a shattered statue of a forgotten king of kings.

pieces.title: The Parthenon Sculptures
pieces.blurb: Gods, horsemen and centaurs from the Parthenon in Athens, and the most argued-over sculptures in the world.
text: The frieze ran round the Parthenon, the temple of Athena on the Acropolis: the procession of the Panathenaic festival, horsemen, chariots and animals for sacrifice, up to the gods seated waiting. Its pediments held the gods themselves, and its metopes the battle of the Lapiths and the centaurs.

From 1801 men working for Lord Elgin, the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire, which then ruled Athens, took down about half of what survived and shipped it to Britain. Parliament bought it in 1816. Greece has asked for the sculptures back since 1983 and built the Acropolis Museum (2009) with a gallery waiting for them.

pieces.title: The Birth of Venus
pieces.blurb: The goddess of love blown ashore on a scallop shell, painted for the Medici.
text: Venus, born of the sea foam, drifts ashore on a scallop shell. The winds blow her in from the left, roses falling round them, and on the right one of the Hours, the goddesses of the seasons, waits with a flowered cloak to cover her.

Botticelli painted it in Florence for the Medici circle in the mid-1480s. It was one of the first big paintings since antiquity of a naked goddess that was not a story from the Bible, and one of the first in Tuscany on canvas rather than on wood.

pieces.title: Primavera
pieces.blurb: Venus in her orange grove with the three Graces, Flora and the winds of spring.
text: In a dark grove of orange trees, Venus stands in the middle with Cupid aiming his arrow over her head. On the left the three Graces dance and Mercury pokes at the clouds; on the right Zephyr, the west wind, catches the nymph Chloris, who turns into Flora, strewing flowers in her painted dress.
It hung in a Medici house in Florence. Botanists have counted some 500 plants on its meadow, about 190 of them different flowers, nearly all of them ones that bloom around Florence in spring.

pieces.title: Venus de’ Medici
pieces.blurb: The marble goddess in the middle of the Tribuna, once the most admired statue in Europe.
text: Venus turns as if surprised while bathing, a dolphin at her feet. A Greek sculptor carved her in the first century BC, after the Aphrodite of Knidos of Praxiteles; the base names Kleomenes, son of Apollodoros, of Athens.

The Medici kept her in their villa in Rome and brought her to Florence in 1677, to the red-velvet octagon of the Tribuna. Travellers on the Grand Tour came to see her above all else. Napoleon took her to Paris in 1802; she came back in 1815.

pieces.title: The Annunciation
pieces.blurb: The angel Gabriel kneels in a garden to tell the Virgin she will bear a son.
text: Leonardo painted it in his early twenties, still in the workshop of his master Verrocchio. Gabriel's wings were first painted after a real bird's; another hand made them longer later.
It came to the Uffizi in 1867 from a monastery near Florence, as a Ghirlandaio. Only in 1869 did critics recognise the young Leonardo in it.

pieces.title: Venus of Urbino
pieces.blurb: A young woman lying on a bed looks straight out at us, her little dog asleep at her feet, two maids at a chest behind.
text: Titian painted it for Guidobaldo della Rovere, soon Duke of Urbino, who called it simply the naked woman. The maids looking for her clothes in the chest and the sleeping dog make it a bedroom in Venice rather than a goddess's grove.
Mark Twain called it the vilest picture in the world; Manet answered it with his Olympia in 1863, the same pose, the same frank look.

pieces.title: Medusa
pieces.medium: Oil on canvas on a wooden shield
pieces.blurb: The Gorgon's head at the moment Perseus cuts it off, screaming, snakes for hair, on a round parade shield.
text: Cardinal Francesco Maria del Monte had it made as a gift for Ferdinando I de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany: a ceremonial shield, the monster whose look turned men to stone painted on it.
The shield is convex, but Caravaggio painted it as if it were flat and dished, the head standing out from it, still alive, blood spurting. It is said to be his own face.

pieces.title: Sir John Hawkwood
pieces.blurb: An English mercenary on horseback, painted to look like a bronze statue on the cathedral wall.
text: John Hawkwood, an Essex tanner’s son, fought for whoever paid best in fourteenth-century Italy and ended up captain-general of Florence’s army. The city promised him a marble monument in the cathedral; when he died in 1394, it never came.

In 1436 Paolo Uccello painted one instead, in greenish earth colours so that the horse and rider look like bronze, standing on a plinth seen from below. Twenty years later Andrea del Castagno painted another condottiere, Niccolò da Tolentino, beside it.

pieces.title: David
pieces.room: At the door of the Palazzo Vecchio, a copy (the original is in the Galleria dell’Accademia)
pieces.blurb: The young giant-killer Michelangelo carved from an abandoned block of marble, the emblem of the Florentine Republic.
text: In 1501 the cathedral’s works and the wool guild gave a 26-year-old Michelangelo a block of Carrara marble more than five metres tall that Agostino di Duccio had begun carving nearly forty years before and given up on; the Florentines called it the Giant. He worked on it in the courtyard of the cathedral’s works, boarded off from prying eyes, until 1504.

He chose the moment before the fight: David has the sling over his left shoulder and the stone in his right hand, his weight on one leg, and turns his head to look at Goliath. The statue was meant for a buttress high on the cathedral, but a committee that included Leonardo da Vinci and Botticelli put it at the door of the Palazzo Vecchio instead, where it was unveiled in September 1504: the young hero who killed a giant, standing for the Republic of Florence against its powerful enemies.

In 1527, in a revolt against the Medici, a bench thrown from a window of the palace broke his left arm into three pieces. In 1873 he was moved indoors, to a tribuna built for him at the end of the Galleria dell’Accademia, and in 1910 a marble copy took his place by the palace door, on the left as you face it, where it stands in the game.

pieces.title: The Creation of Adam
pieces.blurb: God reaches out to give life to Adam, their fingers nearly touching, on the Sistine ceiling.
text: Pope Julius II asked Michelangelo, who thought of himself as a sculptor, to paint the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel. From 1508 to 1512 he painted more than 300 figures on it, standing on a scaffold he designed himself: the prophets and sibyls round the edges, and nine stories from Genesis down the middle.

The Creation of Adam is the fourth of them from the altar. Adam lies on the bare earth, his hand limp; God sweeps towards him in a red cloak full of angels, and the gap between their fingers is the moment life passes over. Some see the shape of a human brain in the cloak round God.

pieces.title: The Last Judgment
pieces.blurb: Michelangelo’s vision of the end of the world, covering the whole altar wall of the Sistine Chapel.
text: More than twenty years after the ceiling, Michelangelo came back, aged about sixty, to paint the wall behind the altar. Christ raises his arm in the middle, Mary beside him; the saved rise on the left and the damned fall on the right, down to Charon ferrying them across the river to hell. St Bartholomew holds up his own flayed skin, and the face on it is Michelangelo’s.

Over 300 figures, nearly all of them naked: so many objected that after Michelangelo’s death Daniele da Volterra was paid to paint loincloths over them, and was nicknamed the breeches-maker. The restoration of 1990–1994 took some of them off again.

pieces.title: The Delivery of the Keys
pieces.blurb: Christ hands Saint Peter the keys of heaven in a great paved square, a domed temple and two triumphal arches behind them.
text: Pope Sixtus IV had the walls of his new chapel painted in 1481–1482 by the best painters of the day, Botticelli, Ghirlandaio, Rosselli and Perugino among them, decades before Michelangelo's ceiling: the lives of Moses on one side and of Christ on the other.

In Perugino's the keys of the Church are given in a vast piazza drawn in perfect perspective; the arches are copies of Rome's Arch of Constantine. His pupil Raphael borrowed the temple for his Marriage of the Virgin.

pieces.title: The Night Watch
pieces.blurb: An Amsterdam militia company marching out, the painting the whole Rijksmuseum was built round.
text: The civic guard of Captain Frans Banninck Cocq commissioned it for the hall of their guild house. Instead of a neat row of portraits, Rembrandt painted them in the commotion of moving off: the captain in black with a red sash giving the order, his lieutenant in pale gold, a drummer, muskets going off, and a girl in gold lit up among them with a chicken at her belt.

It is not a night scene: the varnish darkened over the centuries and gave it its name. In 1715 it was cut down on all four sides to fit a wall of the town hall. Since 2019 it has been restored in a glass room in the museum, where visitors can watch the work.

pieces.title: The Threatened Swan
pieces.blurb: A swan spreads its wings to defend its nest against a dog.
text: Asselijn painted a swan defending its eggs, life size. Later someone added words that made it a political cartoon: the swan is the Grand Pensionary Johan de Witt, the egg Holland, the dog the enemy of the state.
In 1800 it was the very first painting bought by the national art gallery that grew into the Rijksmuseum; it hangs first in the Gallery of Honour.

pieces.title: The Little Street
pieces.blurb: A brick house in Delft, a woman sewing in the doorway, another bent over a barrel in the alley beside it.
text: One of only two views of Delft Vermeer painted. In 2015 a register of what the house owners paid for dredging the canals, from 1667, showed which houses they were: on the Vlamingstraat, where his aunt lived and sold tripe.
Henri Deterding, the oil man, gave it to the Rijksmuseum in 1921.

pieces.title: The Milkmaid
pieces.blurb: A kitchen maid pours milk into a bowl by the window, the bread on the table catching the light.
text: Nothing happens: a maid, absorbed, pours a thin stream of milk, likely for bread pudding. Vermeer made the crust of the bread glitter with dots of light, and painted out a basket of clothes he had first put by the wall.
It is small, only 45 cm high. The state bought it for the Rijksmuseum in 1908, after a debate in parliament over its price.

pieces.title: The Jewish Bride
pieces.blurb: A man lays his hand tenderly on a woman's breast, her hand over his.
text: Nobody knows who they are: a couple of Rembrandt's day dressed up as Isaac and Rebecca from the Bible, perhaps. The name was only given in the 19th century.

Rembrandt laid the paint of the man's golden sleeve on thick with a palette knife. Van Gogh, seeing it in 1885, said he would give ten years of his life to sit before it for a fortnight with only a crust of dry bread.

pieces.title: Las Meninas
pieces.blurb: The little Infanta among her maids, the painter at his canvas, and the king and queen in the mirror.
text: In a room of the royal palace in Madrid, the five-year-old Infanta Margarita stands among her maids of honour, the meninas, with two court dwarfs and a big sleepy dog. On the left Velázquez himself looks out from behind a huge canvas.

In the mirror at the back are King Philip IV and Queen Mariana: they stand where you stand, and the whole scene looks out at them. The red cross on the painter’s chest is the Order of Santiago, which he was given in 1659, three years after he painted himself.

pieces.title: Saturn Devouring His Son
pieces.blurb: The wild-eyed giant eating his child, one of the Black Paintings from the walls of Goya’s house.
text: In his seventies, deaf and disillusioned, Goya painted fourteen dark pictures straight onto the plaster walls of his house outside Madrid, the Quinta del Sordo. He gave them no titles and showed them to nobody. Saturn, the god who ate his children for fear one would overthrow him, hung in the dining room.
Fifty years later a new owner had them taken off the walls and moved onto canvas, and gave them to the Prado in 1881.

pieces.title: The Garden of Earthly Delights
pieces.blurb: Eden, a garden full of naked pleasure-seekers and giant fruit, and a hell of musical torture.
text: Three panels: on the left God presents Eve to Adam in Eden; in the middle hundreds of naked people play among giant strawberries, birds and fountains; on the right is a nightmare hell, where a man is crucified on a harp and a bird-headed monster swallows sinners. Closed, the wings show the world on the third day of creation, in grey.

Bosch painted it in ’s-Hertogenbosch, perhaps for the counts of Nassau in Brussels. King Philip II of Spain, who collected Bosch, sent it to his monastery-palace of El Escorial in 1593, and it has been in the Prado since 1939.

pieces.title: The Third of May 1808
pieces.local: El tres de mayo de 1808 en Madrid
pieces.blurb: French soldiers shoot the people of Madrid in the night, a man in a white shirt flinging up his arms before them.
text: On 2 May 1808 Madrid rose against Napoleon's army; that night and the next morning the French shot the prisoners they had taken. Six years later, when the French had gone, Goya painted the uprising and the executions.

The soldiers are a faceless row of backs and rifles; the man they aim at, lit by a lantern on the ground, holds out his arms like Christ on the cross, a wound in his palm. Its truth about war has been followed ever since, by Manet and by Picasso's Guernica.

pieces.title: The Nobleman with his Hand on his Chest
pieces.local: El caballero de la mano en el pecho
pieces.blurb: A gentleman of Toledo in black with a white ruff, his hand laid on his heart as if swearing an oath.
text: Painted soon after El Greco came to Toledo from Italy, it is the Spanish gentleman as he wished to be seen: sober, proud, his sword hilt showing, his long fingers spread on his chest.
Who he was is not known. A cleaning in 1996 took off old dark varnish and repaint and showed a grey background and a lighter face, to some people's dismay.

pieces.title: The Triumph of Death
pieces.blurb: An army of skeletons sweeps across a burning land, sparing nobody, king or peasant.
text: Bruegel learnt from Bosch, and here the dead overrun the living: they herd people into a great coffin, ring a bell, cut a pilgrim's throat, empty the king's barrels of gold.
Only the two lovers in the corner, singing to a lute, have not noticed yet, and a skeleton plays along behind them. It has been in Spain since the 17th century and in the Prado since 1827.

pieces.title: The Descent from the Cross
pieces.blurb: Christ's body taken down from the cross, his mother fainting in the same curve as his body, ten figures as if carved in a gilded shrine.
text: Van der Weyden painted it for the chapel of the crossbowmen's guild in Leuven: tiny crossbows hang in the corners of the gold tracery. The figures stand close in a shallow box, like a carved altarpiece come to life.
Mary of Hungary bought it, and her nephew Philip II took it to Spain. The Virgin falls in a swoon that echoes her son's body, and the tears on the faces are painted one by one.

pieces.title: The Tower of Babel
pieces.blurb: The tower that was meant to reach heaven, rising in rings of arches over a Flemish port.
text: Bruegel built his tower like the Colosseum in Rome, which he had seen, ring upon ring of arches spiralling up into the clouds, already crumbling at the bottom before the top is finished. Around it lies a busy Flemish harbour like Antwerp’s, ships unloading stone.

In the corner King Nimrod, who ordered it built, visits the stonemasons, who kneel before him. Thousands of tiny workers swarm over it, with cranes, ladders and scaffolding. A smaller version by Bruegel hangs in Rotterdam.

pieces.title: The Hunters in the Snow
pieces.blurb: Three tired hunters coming home over the snowy hill, the village below skating on the ice.
text: Three hunters and their dogs trudge down the hill past bare trees, with just one fox to show for the day. Below them the frozen ponds are full of skaters, curlers and children with spinning tops, under a cold grey-green sky.
It is one of a series of six paintings of the times of the year that the Antwerp merchant Niclaes Jongelinck ordered for his house; five survive, and three of them hang in Vienna.

pieces.title: The Peasant Wedding
pieces.blurb: A crowded wedding feast in a barn, the bride under her paper crown.
text: The guests crowd round a long table in a barn, the bride sitting smugly under a paper crown in front of a green cloth. Two men carry in bowls of porridge on a door taken off its hinges, a bagpiper looks hungrily at the food and a child in a big hat licks a plate clean.
Nobody is sure which one is the groom. Bruegel painted the people of the Flemish countryside like this, eating, dancing and fighting, so often that he was called Peasant Bruegel.

pieces.title: Children's Games
pieces.blurb: A whole town given over to children at play, some 80 games at once.
text: Some two hundred children fill a square and a street: hoops, stilts, leapfrog, blind man's buff, knucklebones, playing at weddings and at church. Historians have counted around eighty games, many still played.
Archduke Ernst of Austria bought it in 1594, and it has been in the Habsburgs' collection, now this museum, ever since.

pieces.title: The Fight Between Carnival and Lent
pieces.local: Der Kampf zwischen Fasching und Fasten
pieces.blurb: A fat man astride a barrel jousts with a thin old woman on a cart: Carnival against Lent, in a crowded town square.
text: Carnival, with a pie on his head and a spit of roast meat for a lance, rides out from the inn on the left; Lent, on her cart pulled by a monk and a nun, holds out a baker's paddle with two herrings on it, from the church on the right.
Round them the whole town feasts, begs, sells fish, plays and prays: the day before Ash Wednesday, the fat days giving way to the lean.

pieces.title: The Art of Painting
pieces.blurb: A painter seen from behind paints a young woman dressed as Clio, the muse of history, a great map of the Netherlands on the wall.
text: Behind a heavy curtain we look over a painter's shoulder as he begins the laurel wreath of his model, Clio, with her trumpet and her book. The map shows the Netherlands still whole, before they split.
Vermeer kept it all his life, and his widow tried to save it from his creditors. Hitler bought it in 1940 for the museum he planned in Linz; after the war it came to this museum.

pieces.title: Bust of Nefertiti
pieces.blurb: The painted queen of Egypt, found in a sculptor’s workshop where she had stood for 3,300 years.
text: Nefertiti was the great royal wife of the pharaoh Akhenaten, who moved Egypt’s capital to a new city at Amarna. Her bust, with its tall blue crown, was probably a model for other portraits of her, which is why one eye was never inlaid.

A German expedition led by Ludwig Borchardt found it on 6 December 1912 in the ruins of the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose. It has been in Berlin since 1913, on show since 1924, and Egypt has asked for it back many times.

pieces.title: The Pergamon Altar
pieces.blurb: A whole Greek altar with its battle of the gods and the giants, rebuilt inside a museum.
text: King Eumenes II built the altar on the acropolis of Pergamon, in what is now western Turkey, in the first half of the second century BC. Round its base runs a frieze 113 m long of the gods fighting the giants, figures more than life-size twisting out of the marble.
The German engineer Carl Humann dug it up from 1878 and the pieces went to Berlin, where the museum was built round it. The hall is closed for rebuilding until about 2027.

pieces.title: The Ishtar Gate
pieces.blurb: The blue-glazed gate of Babylon, with its lions, bulls and dragons, at the end of the Processional Way.
text: King Nebuchadnezzar II built it around 575 BC as the eighth gate into Babylon, dedicated to the goddess Ishtar. Its bricks are glazed deep blue, with rows of bulls and dragons in yellow and white; the walls of the Processional Way leading up to it are lined with lions.

Robert Koldewey’s German expedition dug up the fragments from 1902 and the museum put the gate together again from them in the 1930s. Only the smaller front gate is here: the larger one behind it was too tall for the building.

pieces.title: The Pala d’Oro
pieces.medium: Gold, silver gilt, enamel, pearls and gems
pieces.blurb: The golden altarpiece of St Mark’s, made over four centuries from Byzantine enamels and gems.
text: The doge Pietro Orseolo ordered the first one from Constantinople in 976. It was enlarged in 1105, again in 1209 with enamels looted from Constantinople by the crusaders in 1204, and given its Gothic gold frame by the goldsmith Giovanni Paolo Boninsegna in 1345.

About 250 enamels of Christ, saints and prophets sit in it among almost two thousand pearls and gemstones. It stands behind the high altar, over the tomb of St Mark himself, and on feast days it is turned round to face the church.

pieces.title: The Ghent Altarpiece
pieces.room: Its own chapel, at the back
pieces.blurb: The Adoration of the Mystic Lamb, the Van Eyck brothers’ masterpiece and the most stolen painting in the world.
text: Joos Vijd and his wife Elisabeth Borluut paid for it for their chapel in the church of St John, now St Bavo’s. The verse on its frame says Hubert van Eyck began it and his brother Jan finished it, and it was unveiled on 6 May 1432. Open, it shows God, Mary and John the Baptist above, Adam and Eve at the ends, and below them crowds of saints, judges, knights, hermits and pilgrims coming to worship the Lamb on an altar in a meadow full of flowers.

Few paintings have had more adventures. Napoleon took the middle panels to the Louvre; the wings were sold and hung in Berlin until the Treaty of Versailles brought them back in 1920. In 1934 the panel of the Just Judges was stolen, and it has never been found. The Nazis carried the rest off to a salt mine in Austria, where the Monuments Men found it in 1945.
A restoration since 2012 took off centuries of overpainting, and in 2020 the Lamb looked out again with the strangely human face the Van Eycks gave it.
